So, before I get to answering specific questions, let's have a bit of a primer.

LAN stands for "Local Area Network". In the simplest case, a LAN does not need to be connected to the internet. In a LAN setting, each Network Adapter broadcasts something called a MAC (Machine Address Code) which is a semi-unique set of numbers that differentiate each network adapter connected to the network. MAC addresses are used specifically by the router, and are not broadcast over the internet. In most cases one device will be set up as a DHCP (Dynamic Host Control Protocol) server. This machine, if asked, will provide IP addresses for each computer. There are generally two kinds of IP address that can be assigned - a local IP or a world IP. A local IP will almost always be within certain reserved ranges, such as 192.0.0.x, 172.0.0.x, or 10.0.0.x. A world IP will be assigned by your ISP, and is your identity on the internet.

In the most common configurations where more than one computer is connected to a router, the router will use a technique called NAT (Network Address Translation) in order for multiple machines to share a single world IP. In NAT, only your computer can initiate a socket (there are some conditions, we'll get to that). This means you can call out, but outside things can't call in. When you initiate a communication with a server, the router knows that the socket used for that communication belongs to a specific computer and will forward responses to it. A socket (sometimes referred to as a port) is a network communication pipe. It is generally numbered (1 - 65535). Two computers may not use the same socket on a router at the same time. One computer must give up the socket before the other can use it.

A computer on NAT MAY receive incomming connections if port forwarding or port triggering is configured on the router. Port forwarding means that communications to a specific port will always go to the same machine. Port triggering forwards certain ports to a machine if it first opens a specified port. Another method some software supports is called uPnP (universal plug n play). When this is enabled and supported by a given program it allows the program to tell the router how to configure the ports without any user intervention.

Now, to answer some questions.

1) If you have a router with multiple ports (the thing you plug your ethernet cable in to, not to be confused with a network port), you can plug the machines directly in to the router using standard ethernet cables. There is nothing special to be done here. The only condition is that you should not use any port that is labeled "WAN". The WAN (World Area Network) port is a special port that is used if you have an external modem that provides an internet connection. You'll almost never use this as most modems from ISPs now also double as routers. If you don't have enough regular ports, you will need a device called a switch. A switch is like a dumb router that allows you to split one port in to many. There are different kinds of ethernet cable. CAT-5 is the most common, but you should at least try to get CAT-5e cables if you can. 5e is rated for higher speeds. You can also get CAT-6 and it will work, but it'll be more expensive an unless you're running a 10 gigabit router/switch you won't get any benefit.

2) The short answer is "maybe". This is difficult to answer because it depends on the handshaking method used by the game. Most modern games allow the client to initiate all connections. If this is the case, you will have no problems. If the client attempts to set up a listening socket on a specific port, it's not going to work. Most games do not care if they're getting multiple connections from the same world IP.

3) There are a few different ways to run multiple instances of a game on a single computer. They involve virtualization. The trick here is to run multiple virtual machines on the same computer so they are fooled in to thinking they have their own hardware. For games which require direct access to video hardware (most modern games) this can be problematic since only one game may have exclusive access to a video card at a time. A few industrious people have taken to building computers which have more than one dedicated video card, and then assigning them directly to the virtual machines with a feature found on some mainboards called "hardware passthrough". If supported, this allows a virtual machine to claim exclusive access to a video card even if the host machine has exclusive access to another.

Virtualizing is not without problems. It's complicated, expensive, and time consuming to get right. I would suggest avoiding this unless you have the correct hardware for it and you like tinkering.

EDIT: There is some talk about requiring a "crossover cable" to wire two network adapters together (sometimes called an ad-hoc network) without a hub, switch, or router - I can understand how some might think they need a special cable because at one time you did. However, this is NO LONGER TRUE, and has not been true for over a decade. All modern network adapters implement a system that auto-detects the cable pinouts and modifies their own interface on the fly. This is called Auto MDI-X. Don't run out and buy another cable for this, it will make no difference. There is no benefit to getting a crossover cable anymore - a regular ethernet cable will be fine.
